Forward, backward, nudge. In PyTorch, lo: Go forward to get the loss. Go backward to share the blame. Then nudge every weight. In PyTorch, a coding library, loss dot backward does the middle step for you. Go watch the gradients flow.

Picture the loss as a landscape and the: Picture the loss, our score for how wrong the model is, as a hilly landscape. The weights, the numbers it learns, are a ball on it. The gradient is the slope under the ball. Step downhill by the learning rate times the slope. Then repeat.

Loss landscapes often have long, narrow: Loss landscapes often have long, narrow valleys, like this toy one seen from above. Plain gradient descent, the simple rule from before, zigzags across the walls. It only creeps along the floor. Momentum adds up past gradients, like a heavy ball that keeps rolling. The back-and-forth parts cancel out. The steady downhill part builds speed.
On the real model, the best plain SGD en: Now the real model. The best run of plain SGD, the simple rule we just saw, ends at 0.74. With momentum, it reaches 0.57. That's at a lower learning rate, since momentum sums gradients, which makes its steps bigger.
Here's the catch. At step zero, typical: But here's the catch. The weights come in separate groups, called tensors. At step zero, typical gradient sizes differ hugely between these weight tensors. The biggest is 274 times the smallest. So one learning rate can't suit them all.
Adam keeps two running averages for ever: Adam fixes this. For every weight, it keeps two running averages, updated every step. On top is the average of the gradient. That's the gradient, smoothed out, which is momentum. Below is the average of the gradient squared: that weight's typical gradient size. Dividing one by the square root of the other gives each weight its own step size.
AdamW adds weight decay, a small shrink: AdamW adds weight decay: a small shrink of every weight at each step, applied directly to the weights. This grid shows every run in this one sweep, and teal boxes came close to the best. For AdamW, the biggest good learning rate is 10 times the smallest. For SGD with momentum, just 3 times. Plain SGD never got close. That forgiveness, not needing a perfect learning rate, is a big reason AdamW is the usual default.
Our real recipe also uses a schedule: wa: Our real recipe for TinyGPT also changes the learning rate over time. That's called a schedule. First, warm up for 100 steps. The rate rises gradually while Adam's averages are still noisy. Then decay along a cosine curve. The rate falls smoothly toward zero, so the model settles. The sweep kept the rate constant on purpose.
So: start with AdamW, sweep the learning: So here's the recipe. Start with AdamW. Sweep the learning rate in steps of three, trying each value three times bigger than the last. Warm up, then decay. And if the loss suddenly spikes, turn the learning rate down.

An epoch is one full pass over the train: How much of the data does training actually see? An epoch is one full pass over the training data. Here, that takes about 782 steps. Our 1,500-step runs see each token about twice, on average. But windows are random. So some tokens get seen more often, and some are never seen at all.

Give it more data, and the gap closes. Here are four runs, each with more data. The gap is 1.7 with four thousand tokens, and by 256 thousand it's already gone. Remember, this corpus, our training text, repeats itself a lot.

Delete the x plus from every block of Ti: What lets deep networks train? Take every block of TinyGPT and delete its x plus, the part that adds the input back in. Train on the same data for the same 3,000 steps. The normal model gets its loss, the score for how wrong it is, down to 0.45. The edited one stalls at 4.50, about the unigram level: it only learned which words are common.
And it ignores you. Three different prom: And the edited model ignores what you write. Give it three different prompts, and you get almost the same words back.
Why? Training sends a gradient backward: So why does it break? To learn, training sends a gradient backward through every layer. The gradient tells each learned number which way to move. Without the plus, each layer multiplies it by its own slope, how strongly its output reacts to its input. In a deep stack without the plus, that means multiplying by about 0.2 at every layer. And twenty-four of those in a row leave almost nothing.
Measured in a fresh 24-layer model: with: We measured this in a fresh 24-layer model, before any training. The x plus links are called residuals. And without residuals, the gradient reaching the first layer is 10 to the 17 times smaller than at the top, practically zero. Forward, from input to output, the signal keeps its size. But every position in the text ends up holding the same vector, the same list of numbers. With residuals, the gradient is nearly flat: the first layer gets about as much as the top.
Our 3-layer model isn't that deep: its g: But our 3-layer model isn't that deep. Without the plus, its gradient shrinks only about 130 times. So how stuck it gets depends on the init, the random weights the model begins with. With the standard small init, it stalls. Start the blocks with larger weights, and the same stack, still without the plus, does learn. So residuals make depth easy to train, whatever the init.
The plus sign builds a highway. The sign: So the plus sign builds a highway, called the residual stream. The signal travels straight along it, and each block reads from it and adds its own edit back. On the way back, during training, every plus passes the gradient through unchanged. So even the first layer gets a strong signal.
As blocks keep adding edits, the stream: But as blocks keep adding edits, the stream itself grows. This is where LayerNorm comes in. It doesn't shrink the stream. It hands each block a rescaled copy. It works on one token, one chunk of text, at a time. It subtracts the mean, the average of its numbers, and divides by their spread. Then a learned gain and bias adjust the result. So every block reads inputs of a sane size.
In real trained 12-layer models, the str: How much does this matter? In real trained 12-layer models, the stream grows about 12 times from bottom to top, even with LayerNorm. Without it, the stream grows 165 times. And the validation loss, measured on text kept out of training, ends at 0.69 instead of 0.62, so a bit worse. Remove the residuals instead, and it ends at 4.57, far worse.
So every block is two lines: read a norm: To sum up, every block is just two lines of code. Each line says the same thing: read a normalized copy, then add the result back. Virtually every modern transformer, the design TinyGPT uses, keeps both ideas. There's a residual stream that keeps gradients alive. And there's a normalization layer that keeps sizes sane, either LayerNorm or its simpler cousin RMSNorm.
What does each part of a transformer act: What does each part of a transformer like TinyGPT actually do? To find out, remove it, retrain from scratch, and see what breaks. We try five cuts, and two resizes with fewer or more layers. Each one is trained with the shipped model's recipe, the same settings as the TinyGPT in this app.

The rest look alike by loss, yet their colour scores run from 100 down to 17 out of 100. So a good loss can hide a missing skill. And remember, each is just one run, and runs vary.
So: attention moves information, positio: So, in short: attention moves information between words, positions add word order, and MLPs process each word. Residuals and LayerNorm keep it trainable, and depth lets it build patterns step by step. Now go break one yourself in the Architecture lab.

Plot final loss against size on a log ax: Now plot each model's final loss against its size. The size axis is a log axis, so equal steps along it mean multiplying the size. The dots fall on a smooth curve called a power law. That means every time you multiply the size, the part of the loss above a floor shrinks by a predictable factor. Here it flattens near 0.42, the floor. But that only holds for this token budget, the amount of text we trained on. The same 171 thousand parameter model, trained on four times more tokens, reaches 0.45 instead of 0.49.
Next, plot the same runs against compute, the total work done during training. With a tiny budget, small models win. As the budget grows, the best choice keeps shifting to bigger models. Big labs found the same shape at vastly: Big AI labs found the same shape at a vastly larger scale. In 2020, Kaplan and colleagues showed that loss follows smooth power laws in parameters, data and compute. Then Chinchilla, a study from 2022, looked at a fixed budget. It found you should grow the model and the training data together. Their 70 billion parameter model saw 1.4 trillion tokens, about 20 tokens for every parameter.
By Chinchilla's rule of thumb, derived f: So how do our runs measure up? Chinchilla's rule of thumb was worked out for huge runs on web text. By that rule, our 4 biggest models would want more tokens: the largest saw just 1.7 tokens per parameter. But our data repeats itself a lot, so treat that as a rough guide. And real labs often train far past 20 tokens per parameter, to get smaller models that are cheaper to run.
For your own models: train a ladder of s: What does this mean for your own models? First, train a ladder of small ones. Then fit the curve through their results, and predict the big one before you spend. Balance size and data for your budget. And remember, where the curve flattens depends on the data. GPT-family models, like those behind Cha: How far is our tiny model from ChatGPT? Here is TinyGPT's loop. It reads the tokens, small chunks of text, and scores every possible next one. Then it picks one, appends it, and repeats. GPT-family models, like those behind ChatGPT, run this same loop. And they're built from the same kinds of blocks.
The big difference is scale. GPT-2 range: The big difference is scale. Each bar counts a model's parameters, the numbers it learns. GPT-2 ranged from 124 million to 1.5 billion parameters. GPT-3 had 175 billion, with 96 layers. Its context, the text it can see at once, was 2,048 tokens instead of TinyGPT's 64.
Stage one, pretraining: TinyGPT's game,: Making a chatbot takes three stages. Stage one is pretraining: TinyGPT's game of guessing the next token, played on a huge pile of web text. GPT-3 trained on about 300 billion tokens, and TinyGPT on 12 million. The result is a base model: an autocomplete that may just continue your question. Here it adds more questions instead of answering.
Stage two: supervised fine-tuning. Same: Stage two is supervised fine-tuning, an extra round of training. It uses the same loss, the score for how wrong the guesses are. But now it trains on example conversations written by people: a request, and a good response. The model learns to play the assistant.
Stage three, preference tuning. People r: Stage three is preference tuning. People rank several answers to one prompt. From those rankings, a reward model learns their taste. It then scores the chat model's own answers, and reinforcement learning uses those scores. Learning by trial and reward, it nudges the chat model toward high reward, without drifting too far from its stage two version. That's RLHF: reinforcement learning from human feedback.
In the InstructGPT paper, labelers prefe: How much does this help? In the InstructGPT paper, human labelers compared answers. They preferred a 1.3 billion parameter model tuned this way over the 175 billion GPT-3, which is more than a hundred times bigger.
And a chat is still one long document. S: And under the hood, a chat is still one long document. Special tokens, markers that aren't ordinary text, show who's speaking. And the model keeps predicting next tokens, which form its reply, until it predicts the end-of-turn token itself. That's how it knows when to stop.
Generation's speed trick is the KV cache: Generating text has a speed trick: the KV cache. In attention, later tokens look back at each earlier token's key and value, the K and V. Those old keys and values never change, so keep them, and process only the newest position. For 8 new tokens, that's 30 positions instead of 212, with the same result.
Then the sampling knobs. Temperature div: Then there are the sampling knobs, which control how the next token is picked. Temperature divides the logits, the raw scores, before they become probabilities. A temperature below one sharpens the choice: red gets 96 percent. Above one flattens it: red gets only 72 percent. Top-p keeps the fewest tokens that together cover 90 percent: here, red and white.
So: the same core loop. GPT-3 was a mill: So, to sum up: models like ChatGPT run the same core loop as TinyGPT. GPT-3 was about a million times bigger, with some refinements and far more text. Then it was tuned into an assistant. The core ideas, you've already seen inside TinyGPT.
Inventing a new model isn't one big idea: How do people invent a better model? It isn't one big idea. It's a loop. You start with a hypothesis, a guess you can test. Then you design the smallest experiment that could test it. You set up a baseline, the unchanged model to compare against. You make one change, and run an honest comparison. And only then do you scale up what wins. Let's run this loop, for real, on TinyGPT.
Hypothesis: TinyGPT doesn't need its pos: Here's our hypothesis: TinyGPT doesn't need its position embeddings. Those are the numbers that tell each token, each small chunk of text, where it sits. Attention, where tokens look back at earlier ones, ignores word order by itself. But the causal mask, which hides every later token, leaks some. Each token sees a different number of tokens before it. So maybe the model can work out positions on its own.
The smallest test: short runs of 600 ste: The smallest test is two short runs of 600 training steps, a few minutes at most on two CPU threads. Both use the same code, the same data and the same seed, the number behind the random start. They even see the same batches, the groups of examples trained on at each step. The baseline is unchanged TinyGPT, and the only difference is one line.
Then compare, on held-out text, measured: Then compare the loss, which scores how wrong the guesses are. It's measured on held-out text, kept apart from training, on the exact same batches. Baseline: 0.65. No positions: 0.68. Lower is better, so removing them hurt, by about 0.03.
But one seed could be luck. So we ran tw: But one seed could just be luck. So we ran two more seeds for each arm, meaning each version of the model. Each seed gives its own starting weights and batch order. Both numbers move around, yet every seed agrees: no positions is worse, by 0.03 to 0.04. That gap is bigger than the spread from seed to seed.
Three classic traps. Different compute:: Now, three classic traps. Different compute means unequal amounts of training. Compare against the released model, which trained five times longer, and the gap looks 7 times bigger than it really is. Unfair tuning: the learning rate, the size of each training step, was picked for the baseline, not for the variant. And leakage: 55 percent of the held-out lines, 39 percent of the text, also appear in the training data. So the model may have seen them before.
So at 600 steps, positions win. Now scal: So at 600 steps, keeping positions wins. Now scale it up: more seeds, longer runs, a bigger model, and check whether the gap holds. The app's full 3,000-step ablation, a longer run with positions removed, finds the gap all but closes: 0.450 versus 0.451. And papers report that causal models, which only look backward, can learn position without embeddings. Scaling is where ideas live or die. Your turn: pick a hypothesis and test it.
Want to invent a new kind of model? Here: Want to invent a new kind of model? In the middle are TinyGPT's five parts, from tokens to the generation loop. Here's a map of where people are pushing forward. Each idea changes one part of the engine TinyGPT runs on, and the lines show which part.
RoPE rotates queries and keys by their p: First, RoPE. In attention, each token compares its query with earlier tokens' keys. RoPE rotates both by their position, so attention sees how far apart tokens are. That helps stretch the context, the text a model sees at once, but using very long contexts well is still hard.
Efficient attention approximates or rest: Efficient attention goes after cost. Attention compares each token with every earlier one, so twice the text means about four times the work. Efficient versions approximate or restrict it, like sliding windows that only look nearby, often losing some quality. FlashAttention instead stays exact and just runs faster.
State-space models like Mamba replace at: State-space models, like Mamba, replace attention with a recurrence: they carry a fixed-size state, a running summary, from token to token. So the cost grows linearly: twice the text, twice the work. The open question is how much exact detail that state can hold.
Grouped-query attention lets several que: Next, grouped-query attention. Attention is split into heads that work in parallel. Here, several query heads share one key and value head. That shrinks the KV cache, the keys and values stored from earlier tokens. So generation speeds up, usually with little quality loss.
Mixture of experts swaps the MLP for man: Mixture of experts swaps the MLP, the small network each token passes through, for many expert MLPs. A router picks a few for each token. So the model gets more parameters, or learned numbers, without proportionally more compute: each token only does a few experts' work. Balancing the load across experts is the hard part.
Distillation trains a small student on a: Distillation is about making small models. It trains a small student model on a big teacher model's outputs. Those can be the teacher's full probabilities for every possible next token, or text it generated. The open question is how much skill survives the shrink.
Retrieval-augmented models look things u: Retrieval-augmented models look things up. They search an outside store and put relevant documents into the context, the text the model reads. So knowledge can stay fresh without retraining, as long as retrieval finds the right text and the model actually uses it.
Diffusion language models drop left-to-r: Diffusion language models drop the left-to-right order. They start with every position masked, or hidden, and refine every position over a number of steps. Do they match the quality of autoregressive models, which write one token at a time like TinyGPT, at large scale? That's still open.
Test-time compute spends more thinking p: Test-time compute means more thinking per question, at the moment of answering. The model can write out its reasoning steps, or produce several answers and take a vote. Some recent models are trained with reinforcement learning, learning by trial and reward, to reason longer.
And if you'd rather invent a training fr: And if you'd rather invent a better way to train, that's active too. People study optimizers, the rules for updating the learned numbers. They study data quality and curricula, the order data is taught in. Others try new objectives, like predicting several tokens at once, reinforcement learning after pretraining, or lower-precision math to save memory.
Every one of these changes one box. Pick: To sum up, every one of these ideas changes one box of TinyGPT. Pick a box, form a hypothesis you can test, and run the research loop in the Invent lab.
